stimulus.text:
“Grant that their minds are by nature equal, yet who shall wonder at the apparent superiority, if indeed custom becomes second nature; nay if it taketh place of nature, and that it doth the experience of each day will evince. . . . May we not trace its source in the difference of education, and in the difference of the objects to which the attention of the two sexes is directed?”
— Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” Massachusetts Magazine, March–April 1790 (written 1779; abridged)
stimulus.source_note: Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” Massachusetts Magazine, March-April 1790. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes” (1790), public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, B. Evolving Ideas on Gender

primary_sources: Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes” (1790)

stem: Compared with the idea of republican motherhood, Murray's argument goes further in that it claims

options.text: Women should be educated only so they can raise virtuous sons
options.misconception: That is republican motherhood's claim, not Murray's; she argues for women's minds in their own right.

options.text: Women's minds are weaker than men's and need male guidance
options.misconception: Murray argues the opposite: minds are equal by nature, and the gap comes from custom and schooling.

options.text: Women should leave the home and take up public office
options.misconception: Murray never asks for office; her claim is about minds and education, not about leaving the home for politics.

options.text: Women's minds are equal by nature and deserve schooling for themselves

rationales.D: Background: republican motherhood educates women to raise republican sons. Murray says minds are equal by nature, so women deserve serious studies for themselves, not only as mothers.
rationales.A: Raising sons is the republican-motherhood answer; Murray's answer is education for women's own minds.
rationales.B: Weaker minds are what Murray denies in her first line; equality by nature is her starting point.
rationales.C: Public office is not her demand; her further step is about the purpose of education, not about careers.
rationales.general:
1. Name republican motherhood. Background: educate women so they can raise republican sons.
2. Name Murray's starting point. Minds are equal by nature, so the gap must come from custom.
3. Name her further step. Education for women's own sake, not only for their sons' sake.
Remember: two ideas can agree on the means and split on the purpose — ask what the education is for.
